questions.question_text: A quantity satisfies $\dfrac{dM}{dt}=-0.25(M-40)$. What does the number $40$ represent in this model?

options.text: The fixed value that $M$ moves towards.

options.why: Confuses the fixed value $P$ with the starting value $M(0)$, which the equation does not give.

options.text: The rate of change of $M$ at $t=0$.
options.why: Reads a constant inside the bracket as a rate; the rate is $-0.25(M-40)$.

options.text: The fixed value that $M$ moves away from.
options.why: Ignores the sign of $k$; with $k=-0.25<0$ the gap shrinks, so $M$ moves towards $40$.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{dM}{dt}=k(M-P)$ with $k=-0.25$ and $P=40$
Since $k<0$ the gap $M-40$ shrinks, so $40$ is the fixed value $M$ moves towards.

questions.question_text: A pie at $150^{\circ}$C is placed in a fridge kept at $4^{\circ}$C. The pie cools at a rate proportional to the difference between its temperature $T$ and the fridge temperature. Which differential equation models this?

options.why: Uses the pie's starting temperature as the fixed value instead of the fridge temperature.
Writes the difference the wrong way round, giving the negative of the required expression.
Both errors together: the starting temperature is used as the fixed value and the difference is reversed.

questions.solution_text:
The fixed value is the temperature of the surroundings, so $P=4$.
$\dfrac{dT}{dt}=k(T-4)$

questions.question_text: A tray of ice cream at $-16^{\circ}$C is left on a bench in a room at $23^{\circ}$C, and warms according to $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=k(T-23)$. Which statement about $k$ is correct?

options.text: $k<0$, because the gap $T-23$ is negative while the temperature is rising.
$k>0$, because the temperature of the ice cream is increasing.
options.why: Matches the sign of $k$ to the sign of $\frac{dT}{dt}$ without allowing for the negative difference $T-23$.

options.text: $k>0$, because the ice cream is colder than the room.
options.why: Reads the sign of $k$ off the sign of the difference $T-23$ instead of solving for $k$.

options.text: $k<0$, because the ice cream is losing energy to the room.
options.why: Reaches the right sign from a false physical claim: the ice cream gains energy from the warmer room.

questions.solution_text:
While the ice cream is colder than the room, $T-23<0$.
The ice cream is warming, so $\dfrac{dT}{dt}>0$.
A negative difference times $k$ is positive only when $k<0$.

questions.question_text: A quantity satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-0.04(Q-25)$. What is the rate of change of $Q$ at the instant when $Q=90$?

options.why: Substitutes $Q=90$ into $-0.04Q$, ignoring the fixed value $25$.
Uses the difference $25-90$ instead of $90-25$, reversing the sign.
Multiplies $-0.04$ by $25$ instead of by the difference $90-25$.

questions.question_text: A tub of yoghurt at $5^{\circ}$C is left in a room at $27^{\circ}$C, and its temperature obeys $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=k(T-P)$. What are the values of $P$ and of the initial difference $T(0)-P$?

options.why: Takes the size of the gap without its sign; the yoghurt starts below room temperature.
Uses the yoghurt's starting temperature as the fixed value and the room temperature as the starting value.
Uses the starting temperature as the fixed value, then subtracts in the reverse order.

questions.solution_text:
The surroundings give the fixed value, so $P=27$.
$T(0)-P=5-27$
$=-22$

questions.question_text: A lake supports at most $2000$ fish, and the population $N$ obeys $\dfrac{dN}{dt}=k(N-2000)$. When there are $500$ fish the population is growing at $45$ fish per week. What is the value of $k$?

options.why: Divides by $2000-500$ instead of $500-2000$, losing the negative sign that growth towards the capacity requires.
Divides the rate by the population $500$ rather than by the difference $500-2000$.
Divides the rate by the capacity $2000$ rather than by the difference $500-2000$.

questions.question_text: A hot casserole cools in a room at $18^{\circ}$C according to $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=k(T-18)$ with $k<0$. Why does this model say the casserole never becomes exactly $18^{\circ}$C?

options.text: At $T=18$ the rate would be $k\times 0=0$, and the rate shrinks with the gap, so the gap never closes.
Because $k$ is negative, so the temperature keeps falling past $18^{\circ}$C.
options.why: Confuses a shrinking gap with an unbounded fall; while $T>18$ the model keeps $T$ above $18$.

options.text: Because the room temperature slowly rises as the casserole cools.
options.why: Invents a change in the surroundings; the model treats the room temperature as a fixed value.
The expression $k(T-18)$ is defined for every $T$; at $T=18$ it simply equals zero.

questions.solution_text:
If $T=18$ then $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=k(18-18)=0$.
As $T$ falls towards $18$ the difference $T-18$ shrinks, so the cooling rate shrinks with it.
The temperature therefore gets as close to $18^{\circ}$C as we like without ever reaching it.

questions.question_text: A body cools in air kept at $18^{\circ}$C, following $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=k(T-18)$. At the instant its temperature is $78^{\circ}$C it is cooling at $4.2^{\circ}$C per minute. At what rate is it cooling when its temperature is $48^{\circ}$C?

options.why: Treats the cooling rate as constant instead of proportional to the shrinking difference $T-18$.
Divides by the temperatures themselves rather than the differences from $18^{\circ}$C, giving $\frac{4.2}{78}\times 48$.
Scales by $\frac{60}{30}$ instead of $\frac{30}{60}$, so the rate is doubled when the difference has halved.
